docs.title: Rex
docs.text:
A tiny, friendly scripting language for API work. Everything starts with rex. Made in Mzansi. Built for developers who just want to fetch data and print it.

rex.show("Sawubona Mhlaba")

rex.let post = rex.get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1")
rex.show(post.title)

rex.for tag in ["api", "tiny", "mzansi"]
  rex.show("-", rex.upper(tag))
rex.end

Rex is a complete little language: real values, real control flow, real functions with closures, real error handling, and an HTTP client that is part of the language instead of an import you have to remember.

docs.title: Why Rex exists
docs.text:
Most scripting languages make you choose: either a friendly one-liner tool, or a full language with a standard library you have to learn. Rex is the small one that still behaves like a real language.

  • Namespaced by design. Every builtin lives under rex., so your own names never collide with the language and a reader can tell at a glance what is builtin and what is yours.
  • API-first. rex.get, rex.post, rex.json, rex.env and file helpers ship in the box. No dependency hunting for a throwaway script.
  • One file, one command. rex run script.rex and you are done.
  • Honest errors. Every error carries a file, line, column, a caret under the offending token and, where possible, a hint.
  • Small enough to read. The whole implementation is a lexer, a parser and a tree-walking interpreter you can read in an afternoon.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
# functions with defaults, closures and recursion
rex.func greet(who, greeting = "Sawubona")
  rex.return "${greeting}, ${who}!"
rex.end

rex.show(greet("Mhlaba"))
rex.show(greet("Andile", "Hello"))

# error handling that catches network failures
rex.try
  rex.let data = rex.get("https://example.com/api/items")
  rex.show("items:", rex.len(data))
rex.catch err
  rex.show("request failed:", err.message)
rex.end

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install rex-lang
rex run hello.rex

Or from source:

git clone https://github.com/alysiumcorporationstudios/Rex-Programming-Lang
cd Rex-Programming-Lang
pip install -e .
rex run examples/hello.rex

Next: the quick start, the language reference and the standard library.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Rex 1.0.0 is the first release with a stable language surface: the syntax, builtins and CLI documented here are what the 1.x line guarantees. See the changelog for what changed from the 0.1 prototype and the roadmap for what comes next.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Rex is a classic tree-walking interpreter in about 2,500 lines of dependency-free Python (plus requests for HTTP).

source text
    │
    ▼
lexer.py      characters → tokens          (line/col on every token)
    │
    ▼
parser.py     tokens → AST                 (recursive descent, precedence climbing)
    │
    ├──► analyzer.py   AST → findings      (`rex check`, no execution)
    │
    ▼
interpreter.py  AST → values               (scopes, closures, control flow)
    │
    ▼
builtins.py     the `rex` namespace        (60 native functions)

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Module Responsibility rex/lexer.py tokenises source, handles strings, interpolation flags, newline suppression, bracket depth rex/ast_nodes.py dataclass node definitions with line/col, plus to_dict() for rex ast rex/parser.py recursive descent parser; builds the AST; reports syntax errors with position rex/values.py runtime value helpers: Builtin, RexFunction, Namespace, truthiness, equality, formatting rex/interpreter.py Scope, RexInterpreter, statement execution, expression evaluation, imports, limits rex/builtins.py the standard library, assembled into the rex namespace rex/analyzer.py static checks used by rex check rex/cli.py argument parsing, subcommands, exit codes rex/repl.py interactive session, multi-line blocks, :commands rex/errors.py RexError hierarchy and the caret diagnostic renderer

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text:
Everything is namespaced. Builtins live under rex. so a script cannot accidentally shadow show or get, and a reader can tell builtin from user code at a glance. It also means adding a builtin never breaks existing programs.

rex.end instead of indentation. Blocks are explicit. Copy-pasting a snippet cannot silently change its meaning because of leading whitespace, and the parser can point at the missing terminator.

One error type. RexError carries a message, an optional hint and an optional position. Builtins raise it, the interpreter raises it, rex.try catches it, and the CLI renders it. There is no exception hierarchy for users to learn.

Errors are values you can inspect. rex.catch err binds a dict with message, type, line, col and filename, so handling a failure does not require string parsing.

Structural equality that respects types. 1 == true is false. Predictable equality is worth more than convenience in a scripting language people use for data.

Limits, not freezes. A statement budget and a call-depth cap turn infinite loops and runaway recursion into ordinary catchable errors.

Docs generated from code. scripts/gen_stdlib_docs.py writes docs/stdlib.md from the live namespace, and CI runs it with --check. The reference cannot drift from the implementation.

docs.title: Adding a builtin
docs.text:
1. Write the function inside make_stdlib() in rex/builtins.py. Validate arguments with the _need_str / _need_number / _need_list helpers so errors read like the rest of the language.
  2. Register it: namespace["thing"] = Builtin("rex.thing", thing, min, max, "Doc."). Python keywords such as assert must be assigned by subscript.
  3. Regenerate the reference: python scripts/gen_stdlib_docs.py.
  4. Add a test in tests/test_builtins.py.

rex check learns about it automatically, including its argument count.

docs.title: Adding a statement
docs.text:
1. Add a node to rex/ast_nodes.py.
  2. Parse it in parser.py: add the keyword to CONTROL_KEYWORDS, dispatch it in parse_statement(), and add a parse_* method that consumes its block.
  3. Execute it in interpreter.py (_exec), and teach analyzer.py to walk it.
  4. Document it in docs/language.md and docs/spec.md, and add tests to tests/test_parser.py and tests/test_interpreter.py.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
make test          # pytest
make lint          # ruff
make check         # rex check on every example
make examples      # run every example

The suite covers the lexer, parser, interpreter, every builtin, the CLI, the analyzer and every example. HTTP is tested against a fake transport, so the tests run offline.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to Rex are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog and the project uses semantic versioning.

docs.title: [1.0.0] — 2026-11-21
docs.text: The first release with a stable language. Rex is no longer a line-by-line regex prototype: it is a lexer, a parser and a tree-walking interpreter.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Language
  • rex.if / rex.elif / rex.else / rex.end
  • rex.while and rex.for ... in with rex.break, rex.continue, rex.pass
  • rex.func with default parameters, recursion and lexical closures
  • rex.try / rex.catch / rex.throw
  • rex.import "file.rex"
  • lists, dicts, indexing, member access, index and member assignment
  • full operator set with precedence: + - * / %, comparisons, and or not (and && || !), unary minus
  • ${...} string interpolation in double-quoted strings
  • negative list and string indexes
  • block scoping with assignment that walks outward
  • Standard library — 60 builtins under rex.: HTTP (get, post, put, patch, delete, request), files (read, write, append, exists, list_files), JSON (rex.json.parse, rex.json.stringify), text, collections, rex.math, rex.time, rex.env, rex.assert, rex.exit, type conversion.
  • CLI — run, repl, check, ast, init, version, plus --max-steps and --max-depth.
  • rex check — static analysis: unknown builtins, builtin argument counts and undefined variables, without running the program.
  • Diagnostics — every error reports file, line, column, a caret under the offending token and, where possible, a hint.
  • Docs — a documentation site (MkDocs Material), a language reference, a generated standard-library reference, a CLI guide, a formal spec and an architecture page.
  • Examples — 14 runnable programs.
  • Tests — 203 tests covering the lexer, parser, interpreter, stdlib, CLI, analyzer and examples.
  • Tooling — pyproject.toml packaging, make targets, ruff, pre-commit, editorconfig, GitHub Actions CI, a VS Code extension with syntax highlighting.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• rex.get and friends now raise a catchable Rex error on a non-2xx response instead of failing silently, and accept an options dict (headers, timeout, params, json, data, auth).
  • Reading a missing dict key is an error that lists available keys instead of returning null.
  • rex.post(url, data) keeps its 0.1 signature but now accepts an options dict as a third argument.
  • The MIT license file was rewritten to the canonical text so GitHub detects it.
  • Package metadata: Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable, Python 3.8–3.13 classifiers, project URLs, keywords.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• rex/cli.py contained a real newline inside a string literal, so the package could not be imported at all (SyntaxError). The CLI is rewritten.
  • Strings, comments and brackets inside string literals no longer confuse the parser.
  • rex.post with a body containing a comma was split at the wrong comma.
  • Errors inside imported files now report the imported file's name and line.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Every 0.1 program still runs. rex.return at the top level still ends the script; inside a function it returns a value.

docs.title: [0.1.0] — 2026-06-14
docs.text: • Initial prototype: rex.show, rex.let, rex.get, rex.post, rex.return, # comments, one statement per line, ~120 lines of Python.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
rex run <file.rex> [args...]   run a Rex program
rex <file.rex> [args...]       shorthand for `rex run`
rex repl                       interactive session
rex check <file.rex>...        static checks without running
rex ast <file.rex>             print the syntax tree as JSON
rex init [dir]                 scaffold a new Rex project
rex version                    print the version
rex help                       full usage

docs.title: rex run
docs.text:
rex run examples/api_fetch.rex

Everything after the file path is passed to the script as rex.args:

rex run examples/env_args.rex one two

rex.show(rex.args)   # ["one", "two"]

Use -- to pass arguments that look like flags:

rex run script.rex -- --verbose
Flag Default Meaning --max-steps <n> 5000000 statements to execute before aborting --max-depth <n> 200 nested function calls allowed

docs.title: rex repl
docs.text:
$ rex repl
Rex 1.0.0 — type :help for commands, Ctrl-D to leave
rex> rex.let name = "Rex"
rex> "hello ${name}"
hello Rex
rex> rex.for i in rex.range(0, 3)
...> rex.show(i)
...> rex.end
0
1
2

Bare expressions print their value. Blocks can be typed over several lines: the prompt switches to ...> until the block closes. :vars lists what you have defined, :clear forgets it, :quit leaves.

docs.title: rex check
docs.text:
rex check parses a file and runs static checks without executing it. It catches the mistakes that cost the most time:

$ rex check examples/hello.rex
examples/hello.rex: ok

$ rex check demo.rex
demo.rex:2:8: error: unknown builtin 'rex.sho'
demo.rex:5:12: warning: undefined variable 'titel'
demo.rex:9:8: error: rex.len() takes 1 argument(s) but 0 given
  • error: unknown rex.* member, wrong builtin argument count, syntax error
  • warning: reading a variable that was never declared

It exits non-zero when there is an error, so it drops straight into CI:

for f in examples/*.rex; do rex check "$f" || exit 1; done

After a rex.import, name checks for that file relax, because imported names are not known statically.

docs.title: rex ast
docs.text:
Dumps the parsed syntax tree as JSON. Useful when you are curious how something parses, or when you are writing a tool on top of Rex.

rex ast examples/hello.rex | head -20

docs.title: rex init
docs.text:
rex init my-project
cd my-project
rex run main.rex

Creates main.rex with a working example and a README.md. It refuses to overwrite an existing main.rex.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 success 1 runtime error (thrown, HTTP failure, type error, limit hit) 2 syntax error, or rex check found an error 3 usage error (bad flag, unknown command, no file) 4 file not found or unreadable 130 interrupted with Ctrl-C

Scripts can set the code themselves with rex.exit(n).

docs.title: Using Rex from Python
docs.text:
from rex import RexInterpreter

interp = RexInterpreter(argv=["one"])
print(interp.run_source('rex.show("hi")'))   # ['hi']
print(interp.exit_code)

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Rex stays small on purpose, so the bar is simple: make it clearer, keep it friendly, add tests.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/alysiumcorporationstudios/Rex-Programming-Lang
cd Rex-Programming-Lang
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev,docs]"
pre-commit install

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
make test        # pytest
make lint        # ruff
make check       # rex check on every example
python scripts/gen_stdlib_docs.py --check

All four must pass. CI runs the same commands on Python 3.8 through 3.13.

docs.title: What a good change looks like
docs.text:
• Tests first. A bug fix needs a test that fails before it. A builtin needs tests for the happy path and for the error paths.
  • Errors are part of the API. Every new error message should say what went wrong and, where possible, how to fix it.
  • Documentation is part of the change. New syntax goes in docs/language.md and docs/spec.md; new builtins get a docstring in rex/builtins.py and a regenerated docs/stdlib.md.
  • No new runtime dependencies. The interpreter uses the standard library plus requests.
  • Keep it readable. If a change makes the interpreter harder to follow, it needs a very good reason.

docs.title: Adding a builtin or a statement
docs.text: See ARCHITECTURE.md for the step-by-step recipe.

docs.title: Commit messages
docs.text:
feat: add rex.csv.parse
fix: report imported-file line numbers in errors
docs: clarify block scoping
test: cover negative string indexes
chore: bump ruff

docs.title: Reporting bugs
docs.text: Include the Rex version (rex version), the smallest program that reproduces it, what you expected and what happened. If it is a diagnostic problem, paste the full rendered error.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text: Be decent. See CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Fourteen programs live in examples/. Each one is small enough to read in a minute and runs as-is.

File What it shows hello.rex the smallest program variables.rex values, reassignment, interpolation control_flow.rex if/elif/else, while, for, break, continue functions.rex defaults, recursion, closures collections.rex lists, dicts, sorting, aggregation strings.rex split, join, replace, escapes json_tools.rex parse, edit and re-serialise JSON errors.rex try/catch/throw/assert, including network failures files.rex write, append, read, list env_args.rex environment variables and CLI arguments api_fetch.rex GET and read the response api_crud.rex POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, full responses fizzbuzz.rex the classic word_count.rex a small end-to-end report

Run them all:

for f in examples/*.rex; do echo "== $f"; rex run "$f"; done

Or use make examples.

docs.title: A closer look: word_count.rex
docs.text:
rex.let text = "rex is tiny rex is friendly rex fetches json and prints it"

rex.let words = rex.split(rex.lower(text))
rex.let counts = {}

rex.for word in words
  rex.if rex.has(counts, word)
    counts[word] = counts[word] + 1
  rex.else
    counts[word] = 1
  rex.end
rex.end

rex.show("word counts:")
rex.for word in rex.keys(counts)
  rex.show(" ", word, "->", counts[word])
rex.end

rex.let unique_words = rex.unique(words)
rex.show("unique words:", rex.len(unique_words))
rex.show("longest word:", rex.sort(unique_words, true)[0])

word counts:
  rex -> 3
  is -> 2
  tiny -> 1
  friendly -> 1
  fetches -> 1
  json -> 1
  and -> 1
  prints -> 1
  it -> 1
unique words: 9
longest word: tiny

docs.title: A closer look: api_crud.rex
docs.text:
rex.let base = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts"

rex.let created = rex.post(base, {"title": "Rex post", "body": "hello", "userId": 1})
rex.show("created id:", created.id)

rex.let response = rex.request("GET", "${base}/1")
rex.show("status:", response.status, "ok:", response.ok)
rex.show("title:", response.json.title)
rex.show("content type:", response.headers["Content-Type"])

rex.post returns parsed JSON. rex.request returns the whole response: status, ok, headers, json, text and url.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.8 or newer
  • requests (installed automatically with Rex)

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text:
pip install rex-lang
rex version

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/alysiumcorporationstudios/Rex-Programming-Lang
cd Rex-Programming-Lang
pip install -e .

pip install -e . puts the rex command on your PATH and makes the package importable, which is what you want while working on the language itself.

docs.title: Without installing
docs.text:
You can run Rex straight from a checkout:

python -m rex run examples/hello.rex

docs.title: Use it as a library
docs.text:
from rex import RexInterpreter, RexError

interp = RexInterpreter()
try:
    output = interp.run_source('rex.show("Sawubona")')
except RexError as error:
    print(error.render())
else:
    print(output)  # ['Sawubona']

run_source() and run_file() return every line rex.show printed, so you can assert on Rex output from Python tests.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text:
A VS Code extension with syntax highlighting and snippets lives in editors/vscode. It is not on the marketplace yet; install it from source:

cd editors/vscode
npm install -g @vscode/vsce
vsce package
code --install-extension rex-lang-1.0.0.vsix

docs.title: Upgrading from 0.1
docs.text: The 0.1 prototype only understood rex.show, rex.let, rex.get, rex.post and rex.return, one statement per line. Every 0.1 program still runs on 1.0. The one behavioural difference: rex.return at the top level now stops the script (it used to be the only way to end a file, and still works that way).

docs.title: Language reference
docs.text: This is the complete Rex 1.0 language. If it is not on this page, it is not in the language.

docs.title: The shape of a program
docs.text:
A Rex program is a list of statements, one per line. Every builtin and every control-flow keyword starts with rex., so the language is always visible in your code:

rex.show("one statement per line")
rex.let answer = 42
  • # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
  • Blank lines are ignored.
  • Statements end at the end of a line. Expressions may continue across lines inside brackets, after a comma or a binary operator, or after a trailing \.
  • Files use the .rex extension.
rex.let totals = [
  12.50,
  4.00,
  9.99,
]

rex.let sum = 12.50 +
             4.00

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
Type Example Notes number 42, -3.5, 1e3 integers and floats, no separate types string "hello", 'literal' double quotes interpolate, single quotes do not boolean true, false null null the absence of a value list [1, "two", true] ordered, indexable, mutable dict {"name": "Rex"} string keys, insertion ordered function rex.func a value you can pass around and return builtin rex.show native functions on the rex namespace

rex.type(value) returns the type name as a string.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
rex.let name = "Andile"     # declare
name = "Toxic Dee Modder"   # reassign
rex.show(name)

rex.let declares a name in the current scope. Plain assignment (=) finds the nearest existing declaration and updates it, which is how you accumulate inside a loop:

rex.let total = 0
rex.for n in [1, 2, 3]
  total = total + n
rex.end
rex.show(total)   # 6

Assigning to a name that was never declared is an error, with a hint to use rex.let:

Rex Error: cannot assign to undefined variable 'total'
  hint: declare it first with rex.let total = ...

You can also assign into a structure:

rex.let user = {"name": "Andile"}
user.name = "Toxic Dee Modder"
user["country"] = "South Africa"

rex.let items = [1, 2, 3]
items[0] = 99

docs.title: Blocks and control flow
docs.text: Every block is opened by a rex. keyword and closed by rex.end. Indentation is for humans; it is not syntax.

docs.title: rex.if / rex.elif / rex.else
docs.text:
rex.if score >= 90
  rex.show("A")
rex.elif score >= 75
  rex.show("B")
rex.elif score >= 60
  rex.show("C")
rex.else
  rex.show("keep going")
rex.end

docs.title: rex.while
docs.text:
rex.let countdown = 3
rex.while countdown > 0
  rex.show(countdown)
  countdown = countdown - 1
rex.end

docs.title: rex.for
docs.text:
rex.for city in ["Johannesburg", "Durban"]
  rex.show(city)
rex.end

rex.for walks a list (items), a string (characters) or a dict (keys). Numbers are not iterable on purpose, and the error tells you what to write instead:

Rex Error: cannot loop over a number
  hint: use rex.range(0, 5)

docs.title: rex.break, rex.continue, rex.pass
docs.text:
rex.for n in rex.range(0, 10)
  rex.if n == 2
    rex.continue
  rex.end
  rex.if n == 4
    rex.break
  rex.end
  rex.show(n)
rex.end

rex.pass is a no-op, useful as the placeholder body of a block you have not written yet.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
rex.if, rex.while, rex.for and rex.try bodies run in a child scope, so a rex.let inside a block belongs to that block:

rex.if true
  rex.let inner = 1
rex.end
rex.show(inner)   # Rex Error: undefined variable 'inner'

Assignment is different: it searches outward and updates the existing variable. That is why total = total + n inside a loop works, and why you should declare your accumulators before the loop.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
rex.func greet(who, greeting = "Sawubona")
  rex.return "${greeting}, ${who}!"
rex.end

rex.show(greet("Mhlaba"))            # Sawubona, Mhlaba!
rex.show(greet("Andile", "Hello"))   # Hello, Andile!
  • Parameters may have defaults. Defaults are evaluated in the scope where the function was defined, not at the call site.
  • A function without rex.return returns null.
  • Calling with too many or too few arguments is an error, caught at runtime and by rex check.
  • Functions are values. You can store them, pass them and return them.

docs.title: Closures
docs.text:
A function remembers the scope it was created in:

rex.func make_counter()
  rex.let total = 0
  rex.func bump(step = 1)
    total = total + step
    rex.return total
  rex.end
  rex.return bump
rex.end

rex.let counter = make_counter()
rex.show(counter(), counter(5), counter(2))   # 1 6 8

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
rex.func factorial(n)
  rex.if n <= 1
    rex.return 1
  rex.end
  rex.return n * factorial(n - 1)
rex.end

Nesting is capped at 200 calls by default (--max-depth), so runaway recursion fails with a clear message instead of a Python traceback.

docs.title: rex.return at the top level
docs.text:
Inside a function, rex.return leaves the function. At the top level it stops the script, which is how 0.1 programs ended:

rex.show("this runs")
rex.return
rex.show("this does not")

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
From loosest to tightest binding:

Precedence Operators Notes 1 or, \|\| returns the left value when truthy, else the right 2 and, && returns the left value when falsy, else the right 3 not, ! always returns a boolean 4 ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= chained left to right 5 +, - numbers, strings and lists for + 6 *, /, % numbers; * also repeats strings and lists 7 unary -, unary + 8 (), [], . call, index, member

and, or and not short-circuit and accept the symbolic forms &&, ||, !.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
rex.show(1 + 2)        # 3
rex.show(10 / 4)       # 2.5   division always produces a float
rex.show(10 % 3)       # 1
rex.show(2 + 3 * 4)    # 14
rex.show("ab" * 3)     # ababab
rex.show([1] + [2])    # [1, 2]

Adding a string and a number is an error rather than a surprise, and the hint points at interpolation:

Rex Error: cannot add string and number
  hint: join text with rex.str() or "text ${value}" interpolation

Division or modulo by zero is an error.

docs.title: Comparison and equality
docs.text:
<, <=, >, >= work between two numbers or two strings. Anything else is an error.

== and != are structural and type aware: lists and dicts compare by content, and booleans never equal numbers.

rex.show([1, 2] == [1, 2])        # true
rex.show({"a": 1} == {"a": 1})    # true
rex.show(1 == true)               # false

docs.title: Truthiness
docs.text:
null, false, 0, 0.0, "", [] and {} are false. Everything else is true.

rex.if rex.len(items)
  rex.show("we have items")
rex.end

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Double-quoted strings support ${...} interpolation with any expression inside:

rex.let name = "Rex"
rex.show("hello ${name}, 1 + 1 = ${1 + 1}")
rex.show("${rex.upper(name)} in a hole")

Single-quoted strings are literal, which is handy for JSON:

rex.let payload = '{"a": 1}'
rex.let data = rex.json.parse(payload)

Escape sequences: \n, \t, \r, \0, \b, \f, \\, \", \', \/ and \uXXXX.

docs.title: Lists and dicts
docs.text:
rex.let fruits = ["banana", "apple"]
rex.push(fruits, "cherry")      # mutate in place
rex.show(fruits[0])             # banana
rex.show(fruits[-1])            # cherry   negative indexes count from the end

rex.let user = {"name": "Andile", "langs": ["Rex", "Python"]}
rex.show(user.name)
rex.show(user["langs"][1])
rex.show(rex.has(user, "email"))   # false

Reading a missing key is an error that lists the keys that do exist, which is usually faster than debugging a silent null. Use rex.has() when a key is optional.

Dict keys are strings; numeric keys are converted for you.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Rex has one error type, raised by the language and by builtins. Catch it:

rex.try
  rex.let data = rex.get("https://example.com/missing")
rex.catch err
  rex.show(err.message)
  rex.show("at ${err.filename}:${err.line}")
rex.end

The caught value is a dict with message, type, line, col and filename.

Raise your own:

rex.throw "something went wrong"
rex.error("same thing, shorter")     # builtin form
rex.assert(rex.len(items) > 0, "no items to process")

rex.try catches Rex errors, including HTTP failures, missing files and type errors. It does not swallow rex.return, rex.break, rex.continue or rex.exit.

Every error renders with position and, where useful, a hint:

Rex Error: key 'title' not found
  hint: available keys: 'id', 'body'
  --> demo.rex:4:11
  |
4 | rex.show(post.title)
  |           ^

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
rex.import "path.rex" runs another file in the current scope, so its functions and variables become available to the importer. Paths are resolved relative to the importing file, then the working directory.

# lib/greet.rex
rex.func greet(name)
  rex.return "Sawubona, ${name}!"
rex.end

# main.rex
rex.import "lib/greet.rex"
rex.show(greet("Mhlaba"))

Circular imports are detected and reported instead of looping forever.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Default Flag Statements executed 5,000,000 --max-steps Nested function calls 200 --max-depth

Hitting a limit is a normal Rex error, so a runaway loop reports execution limit reached instead of freezing your terminal.

docs.title: Comments and style
docs.text:
# A whole-line comment
rex.let port = 8080   # and a trailing one

Two-space indentation, one statement per line, and rex.end on its own line is the style used by every example in this repository.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text: The formal grammar lives in the spec.

docs.title: Hello, Mzansi
docs.text:
Create hello.rex:

rex.show("Sawubona Mhlaba")

Run it:

rex run hello.rex

Sawubona Mhlaba

rex hello.rex does the same thing. rex run also accepts flags and passes everything after the file to your script as rex.args.

docs.title: Talk to an API
docs.text:
rex.let url = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
rex.let post = rex.get(url)

rex.show(post.title)
rex.show(post.userId)

rex.get returns parsed JSON, so post.title just works. Objects and lists are pretty-printed when you rex.show them:

rex.show(post)

{
  "userId": 1,
  "id": 1,
  "title": "sunt aut facere repellat provident occaecati excepturi optio reprehenderit",
  "body": "quia et suscipit\nsuscipit recusandae consequuntur expedita et cum..."
}

docs.title: Add logic
docs.text:
rex.let score = 82

rex.if score >= 90
  rex.show("grade A")
rex.elif score >= 75
  rex.show("grade B")
rex.else
  rex.show("keep going")
rex.end

Every block ends with rex.end. That is the whole rule: no indentation rules to break, no braces to count.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
rex.for n in rex.range(1, 6)
  rex.show("step", n)
rex.end

rex.for walks lists, strings and dict keys. rex.range gives you numbers.

docs.title: Write a function
docs.text:
rex.func total(prices)
  rex.let sum = 0
  rex.for price in prices
    sum = sum + price
  rex.end
  rex.return sum
rex.end

rex.show("total:", total([19.99, 5.00, 12.50]))

docs.title: Handle failure
docs.text:
Network calls fail. Wrap them:

rex.try
  rex.let data = rex.get("https://httpbin.org/status/404")
rex.catch err
  rex.show("failed:", err.message)
rex.end

failed: HTTP 404 for GET https://httpbin.org/status/404

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Language reference: every statement, operator and rule.
  • Standard library: all 60 builtins.
  • Examples: 14 runnable programs, from fizzbuzz to a text report.
  • CLI: run, repl, check, ast, init.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: Rex 1.0 has a stable language. These are the directions next, roughly in order.

docs.title: 1.1 — ergonomics
docs.text:
• rex.read_json / rex.write_json convenience wrappers
  • rex.map, rex.filter, rex.reduce (needs a lambda form first)
  • rex.retry(n, seconds) for flaky endpoints
  • rex.csv.parse / rex.csv.stringify
  • rex.date helpers on top of rex.time

docs.title: 1.2 — tooling
docs.text:
• rex fmt — a canonical formatter built on the existing AST
  • rex test — a tiny assertion runner for .rex test files
  • rex doc — print a builtin's documentation from the CLI
  • Publish the VS Code extension to the marketplace
  • A tree-sitter grammar for editors that prefer it

docs.title: 1.3 — language
docs.text:
• lambdas: rex.func(x) x * 2 rex.end as an expression
  • rex.match for pattern-style branching
  • rex.foreach with index and value
  • optional type annotations, checked by rex check
  • rex.export for explicit module surfaces instead of include semantics

docs.title: 2.0 — candidates
docs.text:
• a bytecode compiler and VM (same semantics, faster loops)
  • a package registry for .rex modules
  • a REPL with completion and history
  • WASM build for running Rex in the browser

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text:
• classes and inheritance. Dicts plus closures cover the same ground in a scripting language this size.
  • implicit string/number coercion. Explicit is better, and the error message tells you what to write.
  • a package manager before there is a registry to manage.

Have an idea? Open an issue with the enhancement label.

docs.title: Language specification
docs.text: This page is the normative description of Rex 1.0: grammar first, then the rules the grammar cannot express.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
EBNF, as used by the Python reference manual.

program     ::= { statement NEWLINE }
statement   ::= let | assign | if | while | for | func
              | return | break | continue | try | throw
              | import | pass | expression

Newlines inside brackets, after a binary operator or after a comma are treated as continuations and do not terminate a statement.

docs.title: Statements
docs.text:
let         ::= "rex" "." "let" NAME "=" expression
assign      ::= target "=" expression
target      ::= NAME | postfix "." NAME | postfix "[" expression "]"

if          ::= "rex" "." "if" expression block
                { "rex" "." "elif" expression block }
                [ "rex" "." "else" block ]
                "rex" "." "end"
while       ::= "rex" "." "while" expression block "rex" "." "end"
for         ::= "rex" "." "for" NAME "in" expression block "rex" "." "end"
func        ::= "rex" "." "func" NAME "(" [ params ] ")" block "rex" "." "end"
params      ::= param { "," param }
param       ::= NAME [ "=" expression ]

return      ::= "rex" "." "return" [ expression ]
break       ::= "rex" "." "break"
continue    ::= "rex" "." "continue"
pass        ::= "rex" "." "pass"

try         ::= "rex" "." "try" block
                "rex" "." "catch" NAME block
                "rex" "." "end"
throw       ::= "rex" "." "throw" expression
import      ::= "rex" "." "import" expression

block       ::= { statement NEWLINE }

rex.end, rex.elif, rex.else and rex.catch are reserved as block terminators and cannot appear outside a block.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
expression  ::= or
or          ::= and { ( "or" | "||" ) and }
and         ::= not { ( "and" | "&&" ) not }
not         ::= ( "not" | "!" ) not | comparison
comparison  ::= sum { ( "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=" ) sum }
sum         ::= product { ( "+" | "-" ) product }
product     ::= unary { ( "*" | "/" | "%" ) unary }
unary       ::= ( "-" | "+" ) unary | postfix
postfix     ::= primary { call | index | member }
call        ::= "(" [ arguments ] ")"
arguments   ::= expression { "," expression } [ "," ]
index       ::= "[" expression "]"
member      ::= "." NAME
primary     ::= NUMBER | STRING | "true" | "false" | "null"
              | NAME | list | dict | "(" expression ")"
list        ::= "[" [ expression { "," expression } [ "," ] ] "]"
dict        ::= "{" [ pair { "," pair } [ "," ] ] "}"
pair        ::= ( NAME | STRING | expression ) ":" expression

docs.title: Lexical rules
docs.text:
comment     ::= "#" { any character except newline }
NUMBER      ::= digit { digit | "_" } [ "." digit { digit | "_" } ]
              [ ( "e" | "E" ) [ "+" | "-" ] digit { digit } ]
STRING      ::= '"' { character | escape | interpolation } '"'
              | "'" { character | escape } "'"
interpolation ::= "${" expression "}"
NAME        ::= ( letter | "_" ) { letter | digit | "_" }

Escape sequences: \n, \t, \r, \0, \b, \f, \\, \", \', \/, \uXXXX.

Strings cannot span lines; use \n.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
1. A program runs in the global scope.
  2. rex.if, rex.elif, rex.else, rex.while, rex.for and rex.try bodies execute in a fresh child scope of the enclosing scope.
  3. Each rex.for iteration gets its own child scope.
  4. A function body executes in a child scope of the function's definition scope (lexical closure).
  5. rex.let declares in the current scope and shadows outer names.
  6. Assignment updates the nearest existing declaration, or fails if there is none.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text: Eight types: number, string, boolean, null, list, dict, function, builtin. Numbers are a single type; integers and floats are not distinguished by the language.

docs.title: Truthiness
docs.text: null, false, 0, 0.0, "", [] and {} are false. Everything else is true.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Operator Operand types Result + number, number number + string, string string + list, list list - * / % number, number number (/ is always float) * string, number string repetition * list, number list repetition < <= > >= number, number boolean < <= > >= string, string boolean == != any boolean, structural and type aware and or any one of the operands, short-circuiting not any boolean

Any other operand combination is a runtime error.

docs.title: Evaluation order
docs.text: Left to right. and returns its left operand when falsy and otherwise evaluates and returns the right; or returns its left operand when truthy and otherwise evaluates and returns the right.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: There is one error category. Errors carry message, optional hint and optional position (filename, line, col, length). rex.try catches errors raised inside its body; it does not intercept rex.return, rex.break, rex.continue or rex.exit.

docs.title: Execution limits
docs.text: An implementation must abort after a configurable number of executed statements (default 5,000,000) and at a configurable call depth (default 200), reporting a normal Rex error.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text: rex.import expr evaluates expr to a path, resolves relative paths against the importing file's directory and then the working directory, and executes the file in the current scope. Re-entering a file already on the import stack is an error.

docs.title: Reserved names
docs.text: rex is reserved. true, false, null, and, or, not and in are keywords. Everything else is a normal identifier.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Within the 1.x series, the grammar above, the eight types, the operator table and the documented builtins are stable. New builtins and new statements may be added; existing ones will not change meaning without a major version bump.

docs.title: Standard library
docs.text:
Everything in Rex lives under the rex namespace, so a script never collides with the language itself. This page is generated from the interpreter source by scripts/gen_stdlib_docs.py, so it always matches the shipped behaviour.

rex.show("Sawubona")                                    # printing
rex.let post = rex.get("https://example.com/api/1")     # HTTP
rex.show(post.title)                                    # property access
rex.let slug = rex.replace(rex.lower(post.title), " ", "-")
rex.write("post.txt", rex.json.stringify(post, true))

docs.title: Behaviour worth knowing
docs.text:
• Numbers are integers or floats. Division always produces a float; rex.math.round(x) returns an integer when you ask for 0 digits.
  • Strings support ${...} interpolation in double quotes only. Single quotes are literal.
  • Truthiness: null, false, 0, 0.0, "", [] and {} are false; everything else is true.
  • Equality is structural and type aware, so 1 == true is false.
  • HTTP builtins return parsed JSON when the response is JSON, otherwise the response text. Use rex.request() when you need the status code or headers.
  • HTTP errors are catchable Rex errors: a 404 raises, so wrap calls in rex.try / rex.catch when a missing resource is expected.
  • Files are read and written as UTF-8. rex.write creates parent directories for you.
  • Copies vs mutation: rex.sort, rex.reverse, rex.unique and rex.clone return copies. rex.push and rex.pop mutate in place, which is what you want inside a loop.
